title: DataTap: the message that goes to the client about the Jira grant
body:
# DataTap: the message that goes to the client about the Jira grant

Status: **drafted, not sent.** Chris sends it. Nothing goes outside without him.

Owner: CSM. Source of truth for the client wording — `client-note` is internal only and is not
sendable.

Revision 5. Revision 4 plus one required hedge from the CEO on
[DIG-425](/DIG/issues/DIG-425): the claim that the connection cannot delete now says what it rests
on, which is Atlassian's documentation and not a test of Chris's own connection. Revisions 2 and 3
are superseded: the cards bound to them were withdrawn so they could not reach Chris. Revision 4 is
superseded: it is byte-identical to revision 3 and only restored the document title.

---

## What changed from revision 4 to revision 5

Required by the CEO on [DIG-425](/DIG/issues/DIG-425), and the first change to this document since
[@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a) approved it in substance on
[DIG-349](/DIG/issues/DIG-349). No CTO review this time — the CTO's two required lines are untouched,
and this change moves nothing the CTO asked for.

### 1. The delete claim is now attributed, and carries a promise to check — [@CEO](agent://b2f6c4b1-c041-4245-ba1a-73bc5c8f05ee)

Revision 4 told Chris, as fact:

> So unless your Atlassian admin enables them, this connection cannot delete anything on your site.

That is the one property standing between Chris and data loss, and we were asserting it about *his*
connection on the strength of *Atlassian's* documentation. We cannot test it: the grant does not
exist until the admin creates it, which is exactly why [DIG-292](/DIG/issues/DIG-292) is blocked.
So the sentence had one basis and was written as if it had another.

The change is three moves, and it is the same shape as the exposure list four paragraphs above it,
which already says "I am not claiming that list is complete. It is what I found in their
documentation":

1. **Attribute it.** "One piece of good news, on Atlassian's documentation."
2. **Say the hedge.** "on their documentation, unless your Atlassian admin enables them" — the
   condition now hangs off the source as well as off the admin.
3. **Promise the check.** We check it on the live grant before the first write and tell him what we
   find. A hedge with nothing behind it is decoration; this one has a job attached.

The third move says what happens if the check comes back bad: if delete turns out to be available to
the account, we stop and talk before anything is written. That is not a new commitment — it is
weaker than the "we will not write to your Jira at all until we have put a limit on our side" that
was already in the message and the CTO approved.

### 2. The short chat version carried the same unhedged absolute — my judgement call

The CEO quoted the long version and said nothing else needed touching. I changed the short chat
version too, and I am flagging that as a deviation rather than doing it quietly.

> It cannot delete anything unless your Atlassian admin turns delete on.

That is the identical absolute, in the same document, one screen down. Hedging the email and leaving
the chat unhedged would mean Chris gets a weaker claim on the channel he trusts more. If a message
can be sent two ways, both ways have to be true.

The chat version gets the attribution and the check, compressed to fit its shape:

> On Atlassian's documentation it cannot delete anything unless your Atlassian admin turns delete on
> — I will confirm that on the live grant before we write anything.

### What did not move

Everything else in the client text is byte-identical to revision 4. The unconditional/conditional
split between behaviour and capability is unchanged, and so is every one of the CTO's two required
lines.

---

## What changed from revision 2 to revision 3

Revision 2 was approved in substance by [@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a) on
[DIG-349](/DIG/issues/DIG-349). Two lines were required before it goes, and both are in. Nothing else
in revision 2 moved.

### 1. "A limit" is now defined — [@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a)

Revision 2 said we would not write to the client Jira *"until we have put a limit on our side and you
have agreed to it"*, and never said what a limit is. The sentence we were both most careful about
sat immediately after that one, which left the CTO's own deliberately-open path — connect early, rely
on the human-confirm step — readable as satisfying "a limit". A reasonable reader, including us in six
months, could take the confirm step for the limit and write to a client ticket against a promise not
to.

The sentence the CTO supplied is in verbatim, so the client and any future agent both read the same
definition:

> we will not write to your Jira at all until we have put a limit on our side — that is, we configure
> the connection so that adding a comment is the only thing it can do — and you have agreed to it.

This closes the path rather than leaving it open. It costs one clause and it is the clause that makes
the rest of the message load-bearing.

### 2. The narrowing line — [@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a), drafted by [@FDE DataTap](agent://67fc3794-de10-42aa-830d-3fefb3b491e1)

Revision 2 disclosed every surface it could find beyond Jira and never said we were asking for less. As
written we would tell DataTap all of that and then request a grant carrying it, which is the worst of
both worlds: maximum disclosure, maximum ask. The sentence the FDE drafted is in, at the end of the
exposure list:

> We are asking your administrator for the Jira write permission only, so those other products are
> out of scope.

I have placed it **after** "I am not claiming that list is complete" and before the good-news
paragraph, so the sentences read in the order that is true: *this is what such a grant can reach* →
*this is what we are actually asking for* → *and here is the part that is switched off*.

It also gives the client something to do with the bad news. Revision 2 told DataTap about surfaces
they did not ask about and then asked them for nothing narrower. Revision 3 turns that same paragraph
into the reason the ask is small, which is a better answer than the one it replaced.

### 3. Optional softening, taken — [@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a)

*"cannot reach another site"* → *"is bound to your site"*. It was the same kind of absolute claim we
spent the day removing, and the softer version is the one Atlassian's own documentation supports.

### 4. One consistency fix of mine, flagged because the CTO said nothing else needed to move

The short chat version said the connection *"reaches Confluence and Bitbucket too"*. With the
narrowing line now in the long version, a client reading only the chat message could believe we are
requesting Confluence write access. I added *"though we ask for the Jira part only"* to the short
version. Nine words, no change of substance, and it keeps the two versions telling the same story. I
would rather make this call than ship a chat message that contradicts the email it points at.

---

## The order has changed, and it changed in our favour

Revision 2's header said this message must land **before** the Jira access card. That card is gone.

- The OAuth connection intent on [DIG-283](/DIG/issues/DIG-283), interaction `61674038`, is
  **cancelled**. Nothing is installable.
- The CTO decision card on [DIG-304](/DIG/issues/DIG-304) is **cancelled**. Nothing is waiting on Chris.

So there is no race any more, and the reason to send is no longer "beat the card". It is better than
that:

**Nothing can be connected until [DIG-284](/DIG/issues/DIG-284) merges.** That is the engineering gate
and it has not moved. So sending now costs nothing, risks nothing, and cannot be overtaken by an
approval.

**The message is the only thing on this chain that is not blocked.** [DIG-284](/DIG/issues/DIG-284) is
`in_progress`. [DIG-292](/DIG/issues/DIG-292), Security's scope check, is `blocked`.
[DIG-293](/DIG/issues/DIG-293), the client's named-ticket list, is `blocked`. All three are waiting on
information only DataTap can give, and the two asks at the bottom of this message are exactly that
information: which permissions the authorising account holds, and whether their policy would force
delete or project-admin on.

Sending the disclosure is what unblocks all three. Holding it now holds everything for a day.

---

## The message

Send it in the chat thread, and **also by email.** The action I am asking for is performed by
DataTap's Atlassian admin, who may not be in the chat. Email gives them something to forward.

Greeting carries no name. The DataTap contact is on record only as "Client".

> **Subject: before we connect Jira — what the connection could do**
>
> Hi,
>
> Before we connect Jira I wanted you to see what I found, rather than after.
>
> The connection is an OAuth link to Atlassian's hosted connector. Atlassian documents that kind of
> connection as a general write grant, so I checked what that actually means for you.
>
> **It stays on your site.** It resolves to `codineasy.atlassian.net`, and it is bound to your site.
>
> **It is not limited to one project, and it cannot be made so.** Atlassian says the grant "respects
> the authenticated user's existing access controls and permissions". So its reach is exactly the
> account that authorises it: everything that account can reach on that site, across every product
> your admin has enabled. There is no setting that narrows it to the DCE project, or to any single
> project. I am not going to tell you we can arrange that.
>
> **It is not limited to comments either.** On Jira, adding a comment is 1 of the 15 write actions
> Atlassian lists. Atlassian publishes no way to narrow a grant below one of its permission groups, and
> the finest Jira write group is all fifteen of them.
>
> The same grant reaches further than Jira. Reading their documentation, it also covers:
>
> - **Confluence** write on pages, including changing who can see a page and making a private page
>   publicly readable.
> - **Bitbucket** write on repositories, including merging a pull request.
> - Your **people records** — position, manager and talent records — and who is allocated to what.
> - Your **source code**, through code search.
> - Creating **teams** with open membership, and setting **Loom** video visibility to public.
>
> I am not claiming that list is complete. It is what I found in their documentation. The rule above is
> the part that matters: whatever the authorising account can already do, the connection can do.
>
> We are asking your administrator for the Jira write permission only, so those other products are
> out of scope.
>
> **One piece of good news, on Atlassian's documentation.** Permanent delete is not in the write
> set. Atlassian keeps delete, and project-admin actions, in separate permissions that are off by
> default and only an admin can turn on. So on their documentation, unless your Atlassian admin
> enables them, this connection cannot delete anything on your site.
>
> I have not been able to test that against your own connection, because the grant does not exist
> yet. Before the first write we will check it on the live grant and I will tell you what we find. If
> delete turns out to be available to the account, we stop and talk before anything is written.
>
> Two things would help, and both are before we connect rather than after:
>
> 1. Please leave those two permissions off, and tell me if your policy would force them on.
> 2. Tell me which permissions the account we would connect as actually has.
>
> **Where we are.** Nothing is connected, and nothing has been written to your Jira. That grant is
> wider than I am comfortable handing to software that acts on its own, so **we will not write to your
> Jira at all until we have put a limit on our side — that is, we configure the connection so that
> adding a comment is the only thing it can do — and you have agreed to it.** When that limit is in
> place, the only thing our bots will be able to do is add a note to tickets you name, and we will agree
> that list with you in writing first.
>
> You can revoke the connection from your side at any time, without telling us.
>
> If any of this is wrong for your setup, tell me and we will stop.

### If Chris wants a short chat version

> Hi — before we connect Jira, I checked what the connection can actually do and I would rather you
> saw it now than after. Short version: it stays on your site, but it is **not** limited to one project
> and **not** limited to comments, and it reaches Confluence and Bitbucket too, though we ask for the
> Jira part only. On Atlassian's documentation it cannot delete anything unless your Atlassian admin
> turns delete on — I will confirm that on the live grant before we write anything. Nothing is
> connected and nothing has been written. I am sending you the details by email — two of them need
> your admin.

---

## What changed from revision 1 to revision 2, and who caught it

Revision 2's three fixes are unchanged and still stand. The full reasoning is kept here because it is
what a future agent needs in order to tell whether a future edit is a defect or a preference.

### 1. Two sentences promised a capability, not a behaviour — [@FDE DataTap](agent://67fc3794-de10-42aa-830d-3fefb3b491e1) caught it

Revision 1 ended:

> "so we are putting a limit on our side before we connect. Until that is done we will not write to
> your Jira at all. **Whatever we settle on, the only thing our bots will be able to** add a note to
> tickets you name"

The middle sentence is a promise about **behaviour** and holds no matter what we build. The last one
is a promise about **capability**, and it is only true if the limit actually ships.

That distinction matters, because the CTO's own decision text leaves a path open: *"If you would
rather not wait — a legitimate call, since the grant is revocable and delete is off by default — then
the trade is that the human-confirm step becomes the only thing standing between the model and a
client ticket."* On that path the brake does not merge first, and **"the only thing our bots will be
able to do" is false.** The CTO also recorded the reasoning as *"it commits to a behaviour rather than
a mechanism, so it stays true whichever way the brake turns out"* — the conclusion is right, but that
premise is not, because the sentence commits to a mechanism.

The fix was not to weaken the promise. It was to make it **unconditionally true** and let it close the
gap instead of the gap falsifying it:

- **Behaviour, unconditional:** we will not write to your Jira **at all** until we have put a limit on
  our side — a limit the message now defines — and you have agreed to it.
- **Capability, conditional:** *when* that limit is in place, the only thing our bots will be able to do
  is add a note to tickets you name.

If the brake never ships, there is never a limit, so we never write, and the conditional clause is
simply never reached. Revision 3 adds the definition the CTO required, which also closes the
confirm-step path by name rather than by implication.

### 2. The exposure list was incomplete, and one claim had the wrong basis — [@Security](agent://b14d7a18-99b9-4c04-899b-efdd4676cfd0) caught it

Two separate things, both from Security.

**The basis.** Revision 1 asserted, flatly, *"There is no 'comments only' version of this grant to ask
for."* That conclusion is right, but the citation behind it in the internal record — upstream issue
`atlassian/atlassian-mcp-server#11` — does not say what we said it says. It is titled *"Read-only
mode"*, it is closed, and it contains no `capabilities` parameter and no `READ_JIRA`/`WRITE_JIRA` enum.
The only URL parameter Atlassian documents is `?tools=all`, which paginates the tool list.

So we were establishing "no narrower grant exists" from **the absence of documentation**, while the
wording implied a published capability list. The client may ask "where is that written?" and we would
have had nothing to show. The message now states the basis honestly, in Security's preferred form:
Atlassian publishes no way to narrow a grant below one of its permission groups, and the finest Jira
write group is all fifteen of them. Same conclusion, defensible footing.

**The list.** Revision 1 named Confluence and Bitbucket and stopped. Security found four more
surfaces that were on nobody's list, and two of them are worse for us than the ones we had named:

- `write_confluence` can change **who has permission on a page**, not just make one public. The public
  link was the smaller of the two.
- `write_loom` can set a video's visibility to **public**.
- `write_teams` can create a team with **open membership** — the grant can invite people into their
  org.
- read access to **code search**, and to **capacity-planning and talent records** — who is allocated
  to what, and position, manager and HR records.

Telling DataTap "Confluence and Bitbucket" and leaving those out is the kind of incomplete disclosure
that reads as concealment once they find it themselves. It is in.

The enumeration also got one sentence that stops it being load-bearing: *"I am not claiming that list
is complete. It is what I found in their documentation. The rule above is the part that matters:
whatever the authorising account can already do, the connection can do."* That is Atlassian's own
wording, and it means the next surface somebody finds does not make this message wrong. Revision 3
follows it with the narrowing line, so the same paragraph now also says what we actually request.

### 3. My own framing of revision 1 was wrong

Revision 1's header said the message *"commits only to behaviour — the only thing our bots can do is
add a note to tickets you name — which holds either way."* That is the same error as the sentence it
was defending. The header now says what is actually true and why.

### 4. My own factual error, caught before anything was sent

Revision 1, from the FDE's draft, told DataTap the write grant *"includes creating, editing and
**deleting** tickets"*. That is **false**. Permanent delete is a separate Atlassian permission group,
`delete_jira`, off by default and admin-gated, and it is not part of the write grant — Atlassian's
table does not put `deleteJiraIssue` in the write group. Sent as drafted it reads as a live risk to
their tickets, pulls their security team into a review we do not need, and spends the goodwill we need
for the two asks that matter. Reversed, the delete half is the good news: *this connection cannot
delete anything unless their admin turns it on.* Revision 1 also said commenting was 1 of **14** write
actions. It is 1 of **15**. Small, but the message presents these as Atlassian's published facts, and
an admin who counts the table and gets a different number costs us the whole disclosure's credibility
on a detail.

---

## Not changed, deliberately

- **The two asks.** `delete_jira` and `manage_jira` stay off, and tell us the account's actual
  permissions. Unchanged across all four revisions.
- **The good news about delete.** Still in, and still the strongest thing in the message — but its
  **basis** changed in revision 5. It is now Atlassian's documentation plus a promise to check the
  live grant, not an assertion about Chris's connection. What moved is the epistemic status, not the
  comfort.
- **No name in the greeting.** The DataTap contact is on record only as "Client".
- **No date, no price, no scope.** Nothing in any revision commits us to a timeline or a number.

---

## Rules check

| Rule | How it is met |
|---|---|
| No dates promised | No date, no window, no "soon". |
| No prices or scope promised | None. |
| No internal tools, agents or models | No issue ids, no file paths, no product names of ours. "software that acts on its own" and "our bots" — the client's own word for them. |
| No name in the greeting | "Hi," only. |
| Short, clear, friendly | Opens with what we found, closes with what we need. One clause added in rev 3 to define "a limit", four lines added in rev 5 to attribute the delete claim and to promise the check. |
| One decision for Chris | Send as-is, on chat and email. No card in his queue can race it any more. |
| Nothing false on any path | Behaviour unconditional, capability conditional, "a limit" defined rather than left to the reader, and every capability claim that rests on Atlassian's documentation says so — including the delete claim, which also carries a promise to verify it on the live grant. |
| The ask matches the disclosure | The message discloses what such a grant can reach and states that we are requesting the Jira write permission only. |
